work.title: CREATIVE TREATMENT
work.subtitle: 创意执行提案
work.scope: Fictional community-reading campaign treatment. No brand endorsement, tested audience response, production quote, permissions or approved media placement is supplied.

pages.title: Give the concept a creative task.
pages.lead: This treatment proposes a visual and verbal direction for an imaginary community-reading invitation. Begin with what the communication should help a reader understand, not a promise of campaign performance.
pages.body: The working task is to invite a curious reader into a conversation about a short text. The decision sought is whether this direction is worth developing, not whether a real campaign should be published or funded.
pages.detail: Record a draft response in each labelled field. Keep unknowns visible and distinguish a proposal from an accepted commitment.
pages.question: What should a reader understand after encountering the proposed invitation?

pages.title: State the audience assumption.
pages.lead: Describe the imagined communication situation and what remains unknown about a real audience. A fictional audience sketch is a design prompt, not evidence of demand or a tested preference.
pages.body: The concept imagines an adult who is interested in reading but unsure what a discussion involves. Actual motivations, language needs, access conditions and participation choices would need contextual research before a real campaign.

pages.title: Name the central idea.
pages.lead: A useful concept can be stated simply enough to guide both words and images. The idea should explain the connection between the invitation and the intended conversation.
pages.body: Working concept: a shared page can open more than one perspective. The line is a creative proposition, not a claim that reading produces a measured social outcome. Alternative wording should retain that distinction.

pages.title: Build a short narrative sequence.
pages.lead: Describe how the message unfolds across a beginning, a turn and an invitation. Narrative order helps a reviewer understand the intended experience without assuming a confirmed channel or running time.
pages.body: Begin with a person noticing a passage, turn to two different readings of it, and close with a question about what the reader sees. The sequence is a proposed script, not a record of a real event.

pages.title: Set the visual language.
pages.lead: Explain the role of colour, composition and image treatment in the concept. A visual vocabulary should support the task rather than stand in for evidence about audience response.
pages.body: Cobalt and vermilion can create contrast; close views of paper can keep the text central; two readings can be suggested through different annotations. The supplied watercolor images are illustrative references, not approved campaign assets.

pages.title: Write a sample scene.
pages.lead: Provide enough script detail to make the treatment discussable. Separate proposed copy from production instructions and from claims that would require substantiation.
pages.body: Example scene: a hand rests beside a blank page; a voice asks What did you notice first? A second note offers another reading. This is an invented scene with no actual performer, consent, recording or production arrangement.

pages.title: Adapt the idea by medium.
pages.lead: Show how the same concept could change across a poster, a short sequence or a discussion card. Adaptation should preserve the idea while acknowledging the limits of each format.
pages.body: A poster might centre one question; a sequence could reveal two interpretations; a card could leave space for a response. No media slot, dimensions or real distribution arrangement is confirmed by these examples.

pages.title: Expose production dependencies.
pages.lead: Name the decisions and permissions that would need resolution before real execution. A compelling treatment is not a production quote, license or approval.
pages.body: Dependencies could include final copy, asset rights, accessibility review, responsible production roles and actual distribution specifications. Costs, dates and appointments are deliberately unconfirmed rather than represented by invented totals.

pages.title: Ask reviewers useful questions.
pages.lead: Give reviewers a small set of questions linked to the creative task. This makes feedback more actionable than asking whether they like the artwork.
pages.body: Questions might ask whether the central idea is clear, which line overstates the invitation and which visual cue is unnecessary. A reviewer’s reaction is not a representative audience result or permission to publish.

pages.title: Choose a direction with conditions.
pages.lead: Close with a record of what to develop, what to revise and what to leave unresolved. Choosing a direction for exploration is different from approving final production.
pages.body: A bounded response could request a simpler opening scene and an alternative headline before another discussion. Keep the audience assumptions, image provenance and production dependencies attached when the treatment is shared.
